analysis.one_liner: Requires fracking operations to test nearby drinking water wells for contamination and report results to a public EPA database.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 26 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required oil and gas companies using hydraulic fracturing (fracking) to test nearby underground drinking water for contamination before drilling, every 6 months during operations, and annually for 5 years after. Companies would have to report results to the EPA within two weeks, and the EPA would have to post them in a public, ZIP-Code-searchable database so residents could check their own area. Fracking sites more than a mile from any accessible drinking water source would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations, especially the roughly 17 million Americans who draw drinking water from private wells near fracked wells, would gain the right to know whether their water is being contaminated. The bill gives them test data from EPA-certified labs, searchable by ZIP Code on a public EPA website [S2][S3]. Renters and well owners would not have to pay for the testing themselves; the operator bears that cost.

how_it_helps.text: Requires fracking operators to test all accessible underground drinking water sources within a half mile of the site (or the nearest source within a mile) before drilling begins, at least every 6 months during operations, and at least annually for 5 years afterward, using EPA-certified laboratories [S2][S3].

Requires operators to report results to the EPA within two weeks of each test, and requires the EPA to maintain a free, public, searchable database — searchable by ZIP Code — so residents can easily find test results for their area [S2][S3].

Conditions state control of underground injection programs on adopting these rules: a state must bar fracking unless the operator agrees to the testing and reporting, so states could not simply waive the requirement [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas (and geothermal) companies conducting fracking would pay for the testing, the certified-lab analysis, and the reporting, and would be the source of any contamination data made public [S2][S3]. Those compliance costs are modest relative to the cost of a fracking operation, though operators might pass some of them on. Communities that learn their water is contaminated would face the harder problem of what to do about it — the bill requires disclosure but does not itself clean up pollution or ban it.

drawbacks.text: Testing and reporting are disclosure, not protection: the bill would not stop a company from contaminating water, would not set a standard for cleanup, and would not compensate anyone whose water is damaged — it would only document the damage [S2][S3].

The bill exempts fracking sites with no accessible underground source of drinking water within one mile, and testing is limited to sources the operator can 'reasonably gain access' to — a carve-out critics could use to narrow coverage, since the operator controls access to its own well pads [S2][S3].

The industry's standing objection to federal fracking rules is that states already regulate underground injection and that quarterly testing adds cost and paperwork; the bill also does not address contamination pathways other than the injection process itself [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are modest but real and cheap to deliver: periodic certified testing of water near fracking sites and a public ZIP-Code database cost a company a small fraction of what a single well costs, while the information is exactly what a family on a private well needs. The honest weaknesses are that the bill documents contamination rather than preventing or remedying it, and that the "accessible source" language leaves the definition partly in the operator's hands. On balance it is a low-cost transparency measure that addresses a documented public-health gap: fracking was largely exempted from Safe Drinking Water Act oversight, and this would have closed a piece of that gap [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, where it sat without any hearing, vote, or floor action until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on June 28, 2019, with 15 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S3][S5].
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change — the last action of any kind in the bill's history [S5].
The bill ended with 26 cosponsors, all of them Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committee leadership never moved it, so it never reached a House vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators are better off: they never faced the testing, reporting, or public-disclosure requirements, and no contamination data near fracking sites was collected under this law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators avoiding disclosure

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on and no vote was ever taken, so the bill died entirely within the majority party's committee.

industries.note: Fracking companies would bear the cost of certified testing every 6 months during operations and annually for 5 years after, and would have contamination near their wells documented in a public EPA database. The bill's death means they avoided both the cost and the disclosure. (Geothermal operators were covered too, but oil and gas fracking dominates.)
The bill required all testing to be done by labs certified under EPA's drinking water program, creating paid demand for those services near every fracking site with a water source within a mile.
